In this condition, the transitional probabilities of neighboring syllables were 1.0 within a word and 0.33 between words. The word order was pseudorandomized, such that the same word did not repeat consecutively.

We also created a corresponding random language condition. In this condition, a different set of 12 syllables was concatenated in a pseudorandom order, under the constraint that the same syllable could not consecutively repeat. This yielded a transitional probability of 0.09 throughout the random language condition. The syllables used in this condition were: /da, pø, nu, dø, χo, py, ro, dy, sa, χy, ri, sø/. More details on the methodology used to create these stimuli are described in van der Wulp et al. (2022).

The stimulus lists were converted to concatenated speech without pauses using MBROLA diphone synthesis (male Dutch voice nl2, at a monotone F0 of 100 Hz; Dutoit et al., 1996). All syllables were 300 ms long (100 ms consonant, 200 ms vowel), creating a wordlength of 900 ms. Thus, this yielded a syllable frequency of 3.3 Hz and a word or triplet frequency of 1.1 Hz (see Figure 2). We generated coarticulated speech streams of 13.5 minutes per condition in total, divided over three blocks of 4.5 minutes. Each block was made up of 900 syllables (300 words).

We used GoldWave (GoldWave Inc., 2022) to add a linear fade-in and fade-out of 1.5 seconds at the beginning and end of each block, to avoid a segmentation cue at the beginning of the stream. Stimuli were presented with Presentation (http://www.neurobs.com/). Finally, we used GoldWave to add a cue point 1 at the onset of each syllable in the continuous audio files, so that they could be read as EEG markers with Presentation.

1 For more information about cue points, see https://ils-labs.wp.hum.uu.nl/wp-content/uploads/sites/428/2023/02/cue_points_documentation_ILSwebsite.pdf.

2.3. Procedure

A schematic depiction of the experimental procedure can be viewed in Figure 3. Detailed descriptions of the procedure are provided in the following sections.

2.3.1. Listening Task with EEG

Participants first performed the listening task in the structured language condition. After this, two behavioral tests for SL (rating task and target detection task) were administered, followed by another iteration of the listening task in the random language condition. The listening task was divided into three blocks of 4.5 minutes per condition, yielding 13.5 minutes per condition and 27 minutes in total for both conditions. Participants took short self-timed breaks between blocks. During the listening task, neural responses were measured using electroencephalography (EEG; see section 2.4.1).

2.3.2. Behavioral tasks of SL outcomes

Following the structured language condition of the listening task, participants performed two tasks to assess their explicit and implicit knowledge of the words: a familiarity rating task and a reaction-time based Target Detection Task (TDT).

With respect to the rating task, participants were auditorily presented with a word or foil in each trial. The foils could be of two kinds: one being a part-word spanning a word boundary from the stream, or a non-word made up of syllables from the stream but recombined in an order that never appeared. There were 16 trials consisting of the four words from the listening task, all eight possible part-words and four non-words. On each trial, participants rated on a four-point scale how familiar the word sounded to them (scale: unfamiliar -fairly unfamiliar -fairly familiar -familiar).

The second post-learning task our participants performed was the TDT (Batterink, 2017; Batterink & Paller, 2017 , 2019). Participants were presented (auditorily and visually) with a target syllable and subsequently heard a shortened version of the structured condition from the listening task, containing 16 words (4 words each repeated 4 times) corresponding to 48 syllables, and the same word not repeated in succession.

Participants were instructed to press a button as quickly and accurately as possible upon hearing the target syllable. There were three speech streams per target syllable, with the target occurring four times per stream, resulting in 36 speech streams and 144 targets for this task. Furthermore, participants completed the Computerized Adaptive Beat Alignment Task (CA-BAT; Harrison & Müllensiefen, 2018b , 2018a). In this task, participants listened to the same short musical piece twice, dubbed with beeps. The participant was then asked in which of the instances the beeps were synchronized to the rhythm of the music.

2.3.3. Tasks measuring individual differences in rhythmic ability, working memory, and receptive vocabulary

Participants also completed the Rhythm and Accent sub-tests of the short version of the Profile Of Music Perception Skills (PROMS; Zentner & Strauss, 2017). In this task, the participants were asked to compare auditorily presented rhythms and indicated how certain they were that these rhythms were the same or different.

In addition, we administered the Speech-to-Speech Synchronization (SSS) task (Assaneo et al., 2019; Lizcano-Cortés et al., 2022) Participants were instructed to whisper 'tah' while listening to a syllable stream and to recall afterwards which syllables were presented.

We translated the instructions to Dutch (see van der Wulp et al., 2025).

b. Working Memory (WM)

Participants were administered the forward Digit Span (Wechsler, 2008) as an indication of WM capacity. In this test, the experimenter orally named digits and the participant was instructed to verbally repeat them. The number of digits increased until the participant failed to remember two digit-series of the same length.

c. Vocabulary

Finally, vocabulary size was measured with the Dutch Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, third edition (PPVT; Dunn & Dunn, 1998; Schlichting, 2005). The PPVT is a task where participants are presented with a word and four pictures in each trial. The participant then indicates which picture corresponds to the meaning of the word. The test is suitable for ages 2;3 through 90 years and is norm-referenced for age.

2.4. Data preparation

>Data preparation

2.4.1. EEG recording and preprocessing

During the listening task, EEG was recorded at a sampling rate of 512 Hz using 64 Ag/AgCltipped electrodes attached to an electrode headcap using the 10/20 system. Recordings were made with the Active-Two system (Biosemi, Amsterdam, The Netherlands). Additional electrodes were placed on the left and right mastoid, above and below the left eye, and at the outer canthi of both eyes. Scalp signals were recorded relative to the Common Mode Sense (CMS) active electrode and re-referenced during data analysis to the average of the mastoid electrodes. Electrode offset of each channel compared to the reference electrode CMS was accepted below 20 mV. If the impedance of a channel was higher than this, it was labeled as a bad channel during data collection to be interpolated during data analysis.

The EEG data was analyzed in MATLAB (The MathWorks Inc., 2019) using EEGLAB (Delorme & Makeig, 2004) and the ERPLAB open-source toolbox (Lopez-Calderon & Luck, 2014). The data was bandpass filtered from 0.1 to 30 Hz 2 and 50 Hz notch filtered offline. Bad channels identified upon visual inspection of the data or during data collection were interpolated (mean N of interpolated channels TR group structured = 5.06, random = 6.46; DD group structured = 5.32, random = 7.48). Data sections comprising large artifacts were also identified through visual inspection and manually rejected using the EEGLAB plugin VisEd (Desjardins et al., 2019). A channel was labeled as bad during the analysis if it was labeled as such during data collection due to high impedance, or if it showed frequent noise or drifts upon visual inspection of the data. Following previous work (Batterink & Paller, 2017; van der Wulp et al., 2025 van der Wulp et al., , 2026a van der Wulp et al., , 2026b)), eye movement artifacts were retained. Eye movements were not time-locked to stimulus onsets and have a broad power spectrum that was found to leave the narrow-band neural oscillations unaffected (Srinivasan & Petrovic, 2006).

We time-locked the data to the onsets of the tri-syllabic words and divided the data into non-overlapping epochs of 10.8 seconds, corresponding to the duration of 12 trisyllabic words (36 syllables). We then quantified phase-locking to the word (1.1 Hz) and syllable (3.3 Hz) frequencies using the Inter-Trial Coherence (ITC), which ranges from 0 to 1. An ITC of 1 indicates perfect phase-locked neural activity to a given frequency, and 0 indicates no phaselocking at all to that frequency. The ITC was calculated after a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) for each epoch across frequency bins of interest: between 0.6 to 5 Hz, with a bin width of 0.09 2 Eighteen participants in the TR group and two participants in the DD group had slow drifts in their data.

This made the manual artifact rejection difficult. Therefore, their data was filtered from 0.5 to 30 Hz instead. This did not influence their ITC results at the frequencies of interest. Each block then consisted of 450 syllables (150 words), which corresponds to 2.25 minutes of exposure per block. This enabled us to perform statistical analyses on a combined sample of our data with their DD group (section 2.5.2).

In order to additionally perform an even more fine-grained time course analysis, we followed the methodology of Moreau et al. (2022) using a sliding window to map learning trajectories during the listening task. We created epoch bundles each containing 5 epochs, with each bundle shifted by one epoch (e.g., epochs 1-5, 2-6, 3-7, etc.). This resulted in 54 seconds of exposure per bundle and between 50 and 70 bundles per participant.

We computed the Spearman-Brown corrected split-half reliability for ITCword in the fine-grained time course analysis, splitting odd and even bundle numbers in the structured condition, as well as computing a more conservative split-half reliability using random splits with the splitHalf function from the package psych (Revelle, 2026; see RStudio supplement).

This resulted in a very high split-half reliability of .95 for ITCword during exposure to the structured language condition in the even/odd split. For the random splits, the reliability was estimated at .78 (95%CI = [.67, .86]; see RStudio supplement).

From the bundle analysis, we extracted the maximal ITCword (maxITCword) per participant; the highest ITCword obtained during exposure to the structured language condition. This was the dependent variable for analyses predicting individual differences in SL. We previously took this approach in van der Wulp et al. ( 2025 and 2026a), as we observed in van der Wulp et al. (2025) that aggregated and composite measures such as the mean ITCword over exposure are not as sensitive to individual variation in behavioral SL outcomes as the maxITCword (see also the JASP supplement for the same brain-behavior correlation results with the current data). The maxITCword reflects the participants' peak neural entrainment to the TP structure, and the timepoint at which this peak occurs can differ per individual. Therefore, we hypothesize that maxITCword entails participants' maximum sensitivity to the TP structure during learning, which may be a more sensitive neural marker of SL than an aggregated measure such as the mean ITCword across exposure (van der Wulp et al., 2025).

2.4.2. Behavioral tasks indicating SL outcomes

During the rating task, participants rated the items on a four-point scale from unfamiliar (1) to familiar (4). We compared the groups on their familiarity rating scores (Batterink & Paller, 2017 , 2019; Moreau et al., 2022; van der Wulp et al., 2025 van der Wulp et al., , 2026a)). These are calculated per participant by subtracting the mean rating for foils (both partwords and non-words) from the mean rating score for words.

𝑓𝑎𝑚. 𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝑠𝑐𝑜𝑟𝑒 = 𝑚𝑒𝑎𝑛(𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝑤𝑜𝑟𝑑𝑠 ) -𝑚𝑒𝑎𝑛(𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝑓𝑜𝑖𝑙𝑠 )

We computed the Spearman-Brown corrected split-half reliability for the familiarity rating score, by splitting odd and even item numbers. As there were 16 items in the test, this resulted in an equal split with equal amounts of words, part-words, and foils per half (see RStudio supplement). The resulting split-half reliability was .48 for the rating task.

From the TDT, we calculated a Reaction Time (RT) score per participant, by subtracting the mean RTs to word-final (third) syllables from the mean RTs to word-initial (first) syllables, and dividing this by the mean RTs to the word-initial syllables, which accounts for individual baseline RTs (Batterink & Paller, 2019; Moreau et al., 2022; van der Wulp et al., 2025 van der Wulp et al., , 2026a)).

We also computed the Spearman-Brown corrected split-half reliability for the RT score, by splitting odd and even trial numbers (corresponding to the stream numbers; see RStudio supplement). This resulted in a split-half reliability of .46 for the TDT, comparable to the reliability of the rating task. However, as not all participants hit every target, the amount of RT-data in the odd and even parts of the split differed per participant. Therefore, we also included a random-splits approach which was repeated 2000 times, using custom code (see RStudio supplement). This resulted in a comparable average reliability of .48 (95%CI = [.34, .60]).

2.4.3. Behavioral tasks for individual differences

Assessing RA, the CA-BAT (Harrison & Müllensiefen, 2018a , 2018b) generates a score per participant according to the Item Response Theory. Essentially corresponding to z-scores, a score of 0 corresponds to the mean of the calibration sample and a score of 1 to the standard deviation of the calibration sample's rhythm discrimination ability.

The PROMS (Zentner & Strauss, 2017) yields a raw score for the rhythm subtest (between 0-8) and the accent sub-test (between 0-10), the mean of which we recorded as one data point per participant.

Self-reported musical experience and expertise as measured with the Gold-MSI questionnaire (Bouwer et al., 2016; Müllensiefen et al., 2014) yields a general score between 1-7 for each participant and sub-scores also ranging between 1-7 per sub-scale.

For the SSS task (Assaneo et al., 2019), we adhered to the protocol described in Lizcano-Cortés et al. (2022). We calculated the Phase Locking Value (PLV) for each participant's whispers to the input rhythm of 4 Hz, which ranges from 0 (no phase-locking between the whispering and input) and 1 (perfect phase-locking between the whispering and input).

With respect to the forward Digit Span test (Wechsler, 2008), we measured the longest span for each participant. This test yields a score between 1 and 16, which was recorded as one data point per participant.

Finally, for the PPVT (Dunn & Dunn, 1998; Schlichting, 2005), scores were also recorded as one data point per participant. This score is the age-corrected WBQ (WoordBegripsQuotiënt -'Word Understanding Quotient'), which is a quotient measure similar to intelligence (IQ). The calibrated mean vocabulary score per age is 100, and scores below 100 indicate less-than average performance, while scores above 100 indicate above average vocabulary size for the participant's age.

All scores on the individual differences' tests were standardized before statistical analyses were conducted. This was done by subtracting the mean from the variable, and subsequently dividing that by the standard deviation of the variable.

2.5. Statistical analyses

>Statistical analyses

2.5.1. Bayesian analysis approach

For our statistical analyses, we followed a Bayesian methodology. Bayesian statistical analyses take a different approach to hypothesis testing than frequentist methods. Whereas frequentist significance testing informs us about the likelihood of the observed data under the null hypothesis (H0), Bayesian hypothesis testing allows us to estimate how plausible our alternative hypothesis (H1) is given the data collected. The Bayes Factor (BF) is calculated as follows (Jeffreys, 1961):

The BF10 depicted above quantifies support for H1 over H0. This is done by computing the ratio of the marginal likelihoods of H1 and H0. The marginal likelihood of H1 is 𝑝(𝐷|H1); the likelihood of the data D given hypothesis H1. Likewise, the marginal likelihood of H0 is 𝑝(𝐷|H0) (Nicenboim & Vasishth, 2016). The subscript 10 indicates that the BF10 expresses the support for H1 compared to H0, whereas a BF01 expresses the support for H0 versus H1. In that case, the marginal likelihoods would take opposite positions in the equation above.

To compute the marginal likelihoods of H1 and H0, we fitted Bayesian statistical models to the data that represent H1 and H0, which are then compared to retrieve the BF10.

These statistical models incorporate prior knowledge. The prior knowledge can come from a previous experiment, meta-analysis, or expert judgements. The aim is to include as much prior information into the models as possible, instead of starting the analysis of each dataset as if we know nothing about the topic at all. The prior knowledge is formalized as a probability density function (e.g., a normal distribution, or a Cauchy distribution, etc.

). The hyperparameters of this prior distribution, such as the mean and SD, can be taken from effect sizes of previous research. In our case, the previous research resembling our current study the most is Zhang et al. (2021; discussed in section 1.2). In our preregistration (van der Wulp et al., 2024) we reported our re-analysis of their data in order to estimate the size of their effects using Linear Mixed Models.

These obtained estimates of the effects of interest were subsequently used as a starting point to determine the hyperparameters of the prior distributions for our statistical models regarding the EEG data. In the following sections describing all analyses, we elaborate on each prior distribution used.

In cases where no prior information was available, we used the package Bain (BAyesian INformative hypothesis evaluation; Gu et al., 2023; Hoijtink, Mulder, et al., 2019). Bain computes the approximate adjusted fractional BF by comparing informative hypotheses. These informative hypotheses can be comparisons between, for instance, group means or regression coefficients. Bain does not rely on user-specified prior information, but instead uses a fraction of the information in the data to specify the variance of the prior distribution. Moreover, in the case of unequal group sizes, Bain implements the multiple-population approximate adjusted fractional Bayes Factor, which was shown to be unaffected by the differences in datapoints per group (Hoijtink, Gu, et al., 2019). For more technical information on how Bain specifies the prior distributions, we refer the interested reader to Gu et al. (2014 Gu et al. ( , 2018) ) and van der Wulp et al. (2025).

2.5.2. Statistical analyses of the EEG data

We conducted these analyses with the statistical software RStudio (Posit team, 2024) and R (R Core Team, 2024). We created Linear Mixed Models (LMMs) using brms (Bürkner, 2017), the wrapper package for Bayesian LMMs.

2.5.2.1. Priors

We built the models using the default priors from brms (Bürkner, 2017) for the random effects and intercept. This is a Student's t-distribution with 3 degrees of freedom, centered at 0, with a scale that spreads the values around the center by approximately 2.5 units (weakly informative prior). The heavy tails of this distribution (due to the 3 degrees of freedom) allow for larger deviations from the center compared to a normal distribution with the same scale, which improves model convergence (Bürkner, 2017).

For random slopes, the default prior for the correlations is a uniform distribution. Furthermore, we used a very weakly informative prior N(0, 1) for the residual error (sigma).

For the effect of language condition (structured versus random), we adhered to an informative prior (Silvey et al., 2024) based on the data of Batterink and Paller (2017). We built a LMM on their data (see Data and code availability) and used the estimate of ITCword for condition (β = 0.135) as the SD of the prior for this effect: N(0, 0.135). For the other fixed factors, we adhered to three weakly informative priors based on our re-analysis of Zhang et al. (2021 Zhang et al. ( , 2025;; in: van der Wulp et al., 2024). These priors are normal distributions with the mean set to 0 and the SDs estimated based on the sizes of the effects of Zhang et al. (2021). We then set these SDs intentionally larger to construct weakly informative priors (Gelman, 2006). This was decided because of the limited power of the study by Zhang et al. (2021). The effect might well be larger or smaller in a different sample, and the prior should allow this to be the case (Gelman et al., 2017). These priors are the following: 'narrow' N(0, 0.2), 'medium' N(0, 0.5), and 'wide' N(0, 1). Using three priors with increasing SDs automatically yielded a sensitivity analysis, where the prior is varied by increasing the SD to estimate the robustness of the results against the prior (Nicenboim & Vasishth, 2016).

2.5.2.2. Analyses

The dependent variable was the ITCword (log-transformed and centered due to skewedness; see RStudio supplement). We adhered to the ITCword for the comparison of the DD and TR groups instead of the previously employed Word Learning Index (WLI; Batterink & Paller, 2017) because there are indications that syllable entrainment might be different in DD (e.g., Goswami, 2011; Ladányi et al., 2020; Power et al., 2013). Furthermore, in our previous study including only neurotypical adults (van der Wulp et al., 2025), the results suggested that the stimuli we used -the same as in the current study -encompass less-frequently used syllables in the native language of our participants (Dutch) compared to the stimuli employed in earlier work (e.g., Batterink & Paller, 2017; Saffran, Aslin, et al., 1996). Consequently, this influenced online syllable entrainment and, as a result, the WLI (van der Wulp et al., 2025).

We performed three analyses investigating the time-course of SL: two analyses on the six blocks of exposure, of which one with our data alone and one with the DD group of Zhang et al. (2021) added to our dataset. In the third (final) run, we analyzed our data with the overlapping epoch bundles (see section 2.4.1). In all LMM analyses, we iteratively added predictors and conducted Bayesian model comparison; evaluating the relative evidence for models with versus models without a certain predictor, using the function bayes_factor (Bürkner, 2017; Hu et al., 2023; Nicenboim & Vasishth, 2016). In this case, the resulting BF10 represents the ratio of the marginal likelihoods of two competing models: a model including the predictor (model representing H1) and a model without the predictor (model representing H0). A BF10 > 3 after comparing the models indicates that the observed data are at least three times more likely under the model including the predictor compared to the model without it, providing at least 'moderate evidence' (Jeffreys, 1961) in favor of the predictor's inclusion.

Accordingly, we retained predictors associated with models demonstrating higher marginal likelihoods, as indicated by BF10 > 3, or that were relevant to test our hypotheses, as preregistered (van der Wulp et al., 2024).

We analyzed the time-course of SL using time trends, which were added to the models as factors. For these analyses, we followed a growth curve model approach (Mirman, 2014; 't Hart et al., 2021). All trend components were centered to avoid correlations between trends (Mirman, 2014; 't Hart et al., 2021). We added linear, quadratic, and cubic effects per group and language condition combination (e.g., TR group linear effect in the structured condition).

This helped us to avoid forcing the model to fit, for example, a quadratic effect for all language conditions, including the random language condition, when only the structured language condition might contain a quadratic component. We analyzed the time trends based on the urevents (the syllable number at the start of each epoch bundle, ranging from 0 to 2700) in the EEG data. We used ur-events instead of the epoch bundle number, because our manual artifact rejection method yielded variations in the number of epoch bundles per participant and condition. The data could have been rejected at any moment in the EEG file. As a result, epoch bundle x for participant A could be at a different time point than epoch bundle x for participant B. The ur-events were the same at each time point for each participant, as these were not altered during artifact removal. We standardized the time trend components by dividing the centered variables by their standard deviation, to avoid the confound that the time trends were on very different scales.

All models were fitted by sampling the posteriors in four chains of 10,000 iterations each, of which 2,000 belonged to the warming-up phase. To assess model convergence, we visually inspected the chains, verified that there were no divergent transitions, and that the Rhat values (the between-to-within-chain variances) were close to one. We also ensured that the effective sample size (ESS) was more than 10% of the post-warmup samples (i.e., 800 in our case), following (Nicenboim et al., 2020). See Appendix A.1 for summaries of the model comparisons, and the RStudio supplement for the code of the analyses.

2.5.3. Behavioral tasks and maxITCword indicating SL outcomes

We compared the groups on their SL outcomes using three variables indexing SL ability: (1) the maxITCword, entailing the highest (maximal) ITCword per participant obtained from the bundle analysis of the EEG data in the structured language condition; (2) the familiarity rating score from the rating task; and (3) the RT score from the TDT.

We predicted, in line with earlier studies comparing SL between DD and TR groups (e.g., Zhang et al., 2021) -that the SL outcome scores would be lower on average in the DD group compared to the TR group. We tested these hypotheses with Welch's t-tests in JASP (JASP Team, 2024), using the package Bain (BAyesian INformative hypothesis evaluation; Gu et al., 2023; Hoijtink, Mulder, et al., 2019). We compared the groups on their scores by testing the hypotheses "equal vs. smaller," which corresponds to:

The output from Bain then provides a BF10, as well as the Posterior Model Probability (PMP) for each hypothesis. The PMP for a hypothesis H indicates how much evidence H receives after observing the data out of all hypotheses specified (Hoijtink, Mulder, et al., 2019). The PMPs are decimal numbers between 0 and 1, which add up to 1. In sum, the PMPs indicate the relative degree of support in the data for the hypotheses under consideration. After the initial analysis, we conducted sensitivity analyses. In Bain, this is done by increasing the size of the fraction b of information in the data used to specify the prior variance from 1 × b (default), to 2 × b, as well as 3 × b. If the BF10 does not qualitatively change the result, we can conclude that the results are robust (Hoijtink, Mulder, et al., 2019, pp. 548-549).

2.5.4. Investigating group differences in rhythmic ability, working memory, and vocabulary

>Investigating group differences in rhythmic ability, working memory, and vocabulary

2.5.4.1. Comparing group means

We built a multiple group regression modelfoot_1 in Lavaan (Rosseel, 2012) using RStudio (Posit team, 2024) and R (R Core Team, 2024). We compared whether the scores on the tasks in the model were lower in the DD group compared to the TR group using Bain (Gu et al., 2023; Hoijtink, Mulder, et al., 2019). After the analyses in Bain, we conducted sensitivity analyses by increasing the fractions as described in section 2.5.3. Based on the previous literature regarding SL and RA in DD (section 1.3.2), we predicted that the DD group would show poorer performance on the SSS task, CA-BAT, Gold-MSI, and PROMS. Furthermore, we predicted that participants with DD would have lower scores on the Digit Span (WM; section 1.3.1) and PPVT (vocabulary). This yielded the following hypotheses:

In Lavaan, we operationalized this by recoding the DD group as 1 and the TR group as 0. Then, we created a new dummy variable, which represents the difference DD -TR. If the DD group obtained a lower score on a certain task than the TR group, this variable would be negative.

After that, we specified a model where the difference variable was regressed on all tasks. With Bain, we then evaluated the following hypotheses, with all tasks evaluated together to increase statistical power: • H0: [TASKS] ~ Group difference = 0 -the regression coefficients of the group difference DD-TR for the tasks are all not different from 0.

• H1: [TASKS] ~ Group difference < 0 -the regression coefficients of the group difference DD-TR for the tasks are smaller than 0, indicating that the DD group obtained lower scores than the TR group.

2.5.4.2. Comparing group regression coefficients

After comparing the group means on the tasks measuring RA, WM, and vocabulary, we compared the groups on the magnitude of the relationships (i.e., the regression coefficients) between these tasks and the maxITCword. We again built a multiple group regression model in Lavaan (Rosseel, 2012) with the maxITCword as the dependent variable and the tasks for individual differences as predictors. We then compared group differences regarding the regression coefficients from the model using Bain (Gu et al., 2023; Hoijtink, Mulder, et al., 2019), testing the following hypothesis: • H1: maxITCword~[TASK]DD = maxITCword~[TASK]TR -the regression coefficients between maxITCword and the tasks do not differ between the groups This hypothesis was then compared to the unconstrained hypothesis Hu, which represents "not H1" (Hoijtink, Mulder, et al., 2019).

In other words, we tested whether the regression coefficients for all tasks on the maxITCword were the same for both groups or not.

3. Results

>Results

3.1. Missing and excluded data

One participant in the TR group had missing data for the CA-BAT, PROMS, SSS task, Digit Span, and PPVT. In addition, SSS data of three TR participants were excluded due to technical issues which made score calculation technically impossible. Furthermore, TDT data of one participant in the TR group was excluded because they detected 26.3% of targets, which was below the preregistered 50% threshold (van der Wulp et al., 2024). No data from participants in the DD group were excluded.

3.2. EEG results

>EEG results

3.2.1. Block analyses

We performed two analyses on the EEG data divided over six blocks of exposure: one analysis exclusively on our newly collected data, and one with the DD sample from Zhang et al. (2021) added to our data to increase statistical power. For both analyses, the best model included only a positive effect of condition. Adding the factor group and time trends per group and condition did not improve the model's fit to the data (see the Supplementary Materials and RStudio supplements for the details on these analyses). Therefore, we focus the discussion of our results on the more fine-grained time-course analysis reported in the following section.

3.2.2. Epoch bundle time-course analysis

We analyzed the ITCword as a function of exposure in both conditions using the sliding-window overlapping epoch bundle approach. Each participant had between 50 and 70 epoch bundles, yielding more statistical power than the block analyses (section 3.2.1). Here, we report the model building procedure and results from the best model. For the full model building results including sensitivity analyses, see Appendix A.1.

We have additionally repeated this analysis while excluding the four participants with comorbid ADHD. This did not alter the results presented below.

The model building results and sensitivity analyses for this sample are reported in Appendix A.2.

The null model included a random intercept for participant. Language condition (structured/random) added as a fixed factor highly improved the model's fit (BF10 (0, 0.135) > 1000). Adding language condition as a random slope per participant also drastically improved the model (BF10 (1) > 1000), but subsequent models including condition, group, and time trends combined with these random slopes did not converge. Therefore, we initially left the random slopes for language condition out of the model and added them later again to the best model.

Group (DD/TR) did not improve the model's fit to the data (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.04). However, because investigating group differences was a critical part of the current study, we retained group in the model. We also found evidence for no interaction of language condition and group (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.05), which was then not retained in the model. In the random condition, the quadratic time trend for the TR group improved the model with a negative quadratic effect (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 5.04), which was not robust against increasing the prior (Appendix A.1). None of the other time trends in the random condition improved the model for either group. Thus, the best model at this stage of the analysis included a random intercept for participant, fixed effects of condition and group, as well as a linear time trend for the TR group, a quadratic time trend (positive) for the DD group in the structured condition, and a negative quadratic time trend for the TR group in the random condition.

Then, we continued to estimate the best model for our data. As the fixed factor group had not received evidence that it improved the model, we first continued by removing the fixed effect of group, which improved the model (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 16.42). We subsequently added the random slopes for condition per participant back into the model, which also improved the model's fit (BF10 (0, 0.2) > 1000). We re-estimated the BFs for each time trend and the effect of condition in the model now that the model included random slopes. Removing the quadratic time trend for the TR group in the random condition improved the model's fit now that the random slopes were included, indicated by increasing evidence as the prior increased (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 1.38; BF10 (0, 0.5) = 3.64; BF10 (0, 1) = 7.66). Removing the linear and quadratic time trends in the structured condition for the TR and DD groups respectively did not improve the model's fit and they were retained (linear TR: BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.00, quadratic DD: BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.02).

Removing the fixed effect of language condition resulted in robust anecdotal evidence that removing it would improve the model (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 2.85). This is probably due to the time trend analysis, which estimated trends per condition. However, as we initially received strong evidence that condition improved the model, the difference in model posterior predictive results was very small (see Figure B1 in Appendix B), and this result showed BF10 < 3, we decided to retain condition as a fixed factor in the final model. Finally, due to the large age range in the current study, we included age in the best model. This resulted in strong evidence that age did not affect the results presented above (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.002).

The final model included an effect of language condition (βstructured compared to random = 0.01, SD = 0.005, 95% CrI [0.001, 0.02]), indicating overall stronger entrainment to the word frequency in the structured condition for both groups. The model also included a linear effect in the structured condition for the TR group (β = 0.01, SD = 0.002, 95% CrI [0.006, 0.01]), describing the increase in word-level entrainment as the exposure time increased. Finally, the model included a quadratic effect in the structured condition for the DD group (β = 0.02, SD = 0.004, 95% CrI [0.009, 0.03]), modelling their learning curve in entrainment, initially decreasing, and then increasing in parallel with the TR group (cf. Figure 4).

3.3. Results of group comparisons on SL outcome measures

We compared the groups on their SL outcomes using three variables to assess SL ability: (1) the maxITCword, entailing the highest (maximal) ITCword per participant obtained from the bundle analysis of the EEG data in the structured language condition; (2) the familiarity rating score from the rating task; and (3) the RT score from the TDT. Descriptive statistics for these variables are reported in Table 1. We tested the hypothesis that the group means on these tasks were equal, compared to the hypothesis that the mean for the DD group was smaller than the mean of the TR group. Note. Group sizes are different: TR group N = 118, DD group N = 25. Variance in the DD group is larger than in the TR group. Regarding the maxITCword, we found evidence that there was no difference between the groups (see Table 2). As an extra sensitivity analysis, we also compared the average ITCword in the structured condition between groups, which did not yield different results. Furthermore, removing the four participants with ADHD from the sample did also not alter these results either (see JASP supplement). On the other hand, there was inconclusive evidence on whether the DD group obtained lower scores compared to the TR group on the rating task. The (slightly) larger Posterior Model Probability (PMP) favored this hypothesis (H1) over the hypothesis that the mean familiarity rating scores were not different (H0). However, when the participants with comorbid ADHD were excluded, the PMPs became inconclusive (BF10 = 0.66, PMPH0 = 0.60, PMPH1 = 0.40). Regarding the RT scores from the TDT, we found anecdotal evidence suggesting that the DD group was outperformed by the TR group (H1), which was also substantiated by the PMPs (see Table 2 and Figure 5). This remained unchanged when the participants with comorbid ADHD were excluded from the data (see JASP supplement). When we performed the sensitivity analyses by increasing the fraction b of information in the data used to specify the hyperparameters of the prior distribution (Hoijtink, Mulder, et al., 2019), evidence for H1 increased for all post-exposure tasks, but the evidence regarding the maxITCword remained in favor of H0 (Table 2).

3.4.1. Results comparing group means

In an omnibus analysis, we tested whether there were group differences in the average scores on the tasks assessing individual differences in RA, WM, and vocabulary size. We tested if these means were similar, or if the DD group obtained lower scores on these tasks. The hypothesis indicating that the means on the six tasks were lower in the DD group than in the TR group (H1) received more evidence compared to the hypothesis that the group means did not differ on these tasks (H0; see Table 3).

This indicates that participants in the DD group on average obtained lower scores on the tasks measuring individual differences, taking all tasks together. A visual inspection of the group means and SDs (see Figure 6) suggests that this result is primarily driven by the scores on the Digit Span and PPVT. Mean performance on the CA-BAT was slightly lower in the DD group, as well as self-reported musicality and musical training experience (Gold-MSI). However, as the SDs largely overlap, these differences do not indicate group-level musical or rhythmic impairments in DD. On the other hand, performance of the DD group on the Digit Span and PPVT is around one standard deviation below the average performance of the TR group. This indicates that average WM span and vocabulary size are smaller in our DD group compared to the TR group.

3.4.2. Comparing group regression coefficients

We regressed the tasks measuring individual differences onto the maxITCword, in a multiplegroup regression model in Lavaan (Rosseel, 2012) and compared the coefficients (the slopes of the regression) between groups using Bain (Gu et al., 2023; Hoijtink, Mulder, et al., 2019).

Our hypothesis (H1) specified equality. In other words, H1 specified that the coefficients were not different for the DD group compared to the TR group 5 . We compared H1 to the unconstrained hypothesis Hu indicating "not H1". Although H1 initially received the most evidence, this evidence became weaker in the sensitivity analysis (see Table 4). This is to be expected when evaluating a hypothesis specifying equal means with the approximate adjusted fractional Bayes Factor calculation approach used by Bain, as the smallest fraction b = 1 yields the largest prior variance and therefore the largest support for hypotheses specifying equality. Hoijtink, Mulder, et al. (2019) argue that robust evidence is needed before another hypothesis is preferred over the null hypothesis (i.e., our H1 in this analysis specifying no group Note. All variables were standardized. Error bars indicate the standard deviations.

differences). In our case, the results yield the most evidence for H1, as the PMPs are in favor of H1 over Hu in two of the three fractions.

We visualized the coefficients from the model per group with the 95% Credible Intervals from the model (Figure 7), which indicated that some of the coefficients seem larger for the DD group, others smaller, and again others similar to the TR group. The credible intervals largely overlap, which is probably why we found evidence supporting the hypothesis that the regression coefficients for all tasks combined do not differ between the groups.

3.5. Investigating individual differences in SL in both groups as one population

We found differences between the DD and TR groups regarding their average performance on the tasks measuring individual differences, specifically for WM and vocabulary size (section 3.4.1). These results suggest that the DD group on average shows impairments in WM and vocabulary size, but overlook individual variability within the DD sample (Figure 6). The variance within the DD group on the tasks measuring individual differences overlaps with the variance of the TR group on these tasks. Furthermore, the DD group does not show impairments or delays in SL as measured through neural entrainment (section 3.2). Finally, we did not find robust group differences in the regression coefficients between these tasks measuring individual differences and maxITCword (Figure 7). Therefore, we decided to further explore individual differences in SL (represented by the maxITCword) in both groups combined as one population.

3.5.1. Bayesian Model Averaging analysis

We conducted a Bayesian regression analysis in JASP with Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA; van den Bergh et al., 2021; van der Wulp et al., 2026b). BMA provides parameter estimates for each predictor after considering all possible models with all possible combinations of the predictors. In other words, BMA selects the best model with the predictors that best fit the data.

We followed the methodology for BMA as described in the tutorial by van den Bergh et al. (2021). The dependent variable of our regression models was the maxITCword. Predictors were the scores on the tasks for individual differences (SSS PLV, Gold-MSI, CA-BAT, PROMS, Digit Span, and PPVT). We determined which model was the best model, and what the relative contribution of each predictor was given the data, by looking at the posterior inclusion probabilities of the predictors (van den Bergh et al., 2021).

For BMA, two priors need to be specified. The first prior is the model prior, representing the prior belief that some models are more probable than others. We considered all models to be equally probable, and therefore adhered to the neutral choice of the uniform distribution (van den Bergh et al., 2021). The second prior represents the prior distribution for the regression coefficients: the regression prior. We chose the default Jeffreys-Zellner-Siouw (JZS) prior. This is a multivariate Cauchy distribution on the beta coefficients of the model.

The scale determining the width of the JZS prior is defined by r. We adhered to the default choice in JASP: 𝑟 = √ 18 = 0.354. This is a "medium" scale for the JZS prior (van den Bergh et al., 2021). Sensitivity analyses encompassed varying both the model and regression priors to determine the robustness of the outcomes. Regarding the model prior, robustness was determined with a beta-binominal model prior, adhering to the default settings α = β = 1 (following van den Bergh et al., 2021). This prior assigns equal probability to models with the same number of predictors. With regard to the regression prior, we repeated the analyses with

3.5.2. Results

The best model included the Digit Span and SSS PLV as predictors and obtained an R² of 0.08, indicating that this model accounts for 8% of the variance in maxITCword. The predictors Digit Span and SSS PLV received anecdotal Bayes Factors in the model averaged posterior summary, and their effects were very small (Table 5). Sensitivity analyses by increasing the regression prior to wide and ultrawide did not alter these results (see JASP supplement).

However, the sensitivity analysis concerning the model prior (using the beta binomial prior instead of the uniform prior) yielded the BMA analysis to favor the null model over all other possible models. Also, when we excluded the four participants with comorbid ADHD, or used the averaged ITCword as the dependent variable, the null model became the best model in all analyses (see JASP supplement). Thus, it seems that WM and sensorimotor synchronization comprise positive yet very small contributions to SL in our combined sample, as represented by the maxITCword, leaving most of the variance unexplained.

4. Discussion and conclusions

The aim of the current study was to investigate individual differences in Statistical Learning (SL) for speech segmentation in individuals with Developmental Dyslexia (DD), compared to Typical Readers (TR), as well as investigating individual differences in SL within these populations. Specifically, we hypothesized correlations between Working Memory (WM) and musical Rhythmic Ability (RA) to SL in both groups. We predicted that regardless of diagnosis, RA and WM are positively related to SL. Furthermore, we explored whether SL ability related positively to a larger vocabulary size. We investigated (1) whether the DD group showed poorer SL ability, both behaviorally and neurally, compared to the TR group; (2) whether adults with DD obtained lower scores on tasks measuring RA, WM, and vocabulary size, compared to the TR group; and; (3) whether interindividual variations in RA, WM capacity and vocabulary size similarly related to individual differences in SL abilities in individuals with DD compared to typical readers.

As we did not find differences in on-line SL ability between the groups, as well as no differences in the relations between RA, WM, vocabulary, and their contributions to SL, we additionally explored individual differences in SL by combining both groups into one population.

4.1. No neural evidence for impaired statistical learning in Developmental

>No neural evidence for impaired statistical learning in Developmental

Dyslexia in combination with inconclusive behavioral results

We found Bayesian statistical evidence supporting the null hypothesis that there were no differences in neural measures of SL between the DD and TR groups. During the listening task, both groups successfully segmented the structured speech stream based on the transitional probabilities (TPs). This was indicated for both groups by their neural entrainment to the word frequency (ITCword) in the structured language condition, and absence of such entrainment in the random (unstructured) condition. Furthermore, we derived the maximal ITCword for each participant, and again found statistical evidence that the DD and TR groups reached similar maximal neural entrainment to the word frequency in the structured language condition. These results indicate that our DD and TR groups did not differ in SL as indicated by neural entrainment.

The groups did seem to show slightly different learning curves over time in the structured language condition, as initial word-level entrainment in the DD group was unexpectedly high (cf. Figure 4). This led to a positive quadratic learning curve (initial decrease Mean and SD represent the posterior means and standard deviations of the predictor after model averaging. The final two columns represent the 95% Credible Interval for the parameters.

followed by an increase of entrainment) being the best-fitting time trend for the DD group, whereas the TR group's learning curve was best fitted with a positive linear time trend. These results could be due to differences in group sizes, as the DD group was significantly smaller than the TR group, which increases variance in the time trend estimations for the DD group.

Further research with a larger DD group needs to be conducted to shed light on this issue.

Interestingly, both groups did show highly similar neural entrainment to the word frequency towards the end of exposure: both groups showed a relatively late increase in ITCword in the structured language condition (see also van der Wulp et al., 2025).

This late increase in entrainment for our TR group is incongruent with previous results from Zhang et al. (2021), who found that their TR group followed a quadratic (negative; increasing followed by decreasing) curve, whereas the DD group showed a late increase in learning as measured by ITCword. Both our groups seemed to show a time-course of learning that was similar to the DD group of Zhang et al. (2021). As previously touched upon in van der Wulp et al. (2025), this could be due to properties of the stimuli used in the current project.

Specifically, we used co-articulated speech streams instead of separately recorded syllables, and avoided using syllables that were existing single-syllabic words or frequent forms in Dutch.

This was not controlled for in the stimuli used by Zhang et al. (2021) and related previous work (e.g., Batterink & Paller, 2017; Saffran, Aslin et al., 1996). The relatively infrequently occurring syllables in Dutch used in the current study could have influenced the time-course of neural entrainment in both groups, as they may have been less familiar to the participants.

In contrast to the neural entrainment results, evidence from the post-exposure behavioral tasks used to measure SL outcomes -the rating task and the TDT -was less clear.

The results indicated lower mean scores for the DD group than for the TR group, especially in the TDT. However, the evidence was statistically anecdotal and only became stronger when a larger portion of the variance in the sample was used to estimate the prior in the sensitivity analysis (Table 2). Moreover, the DD group showed variance overlapping with the TR group (Figure 5), which points to individual variability in both samples.

As the behavioral tasks were completed after the familiarization phase, the scores are not only dependent on SL, but also require memory storage of the segmented words and metacognitive decision making (e.g., Bogaerts et al., 2022). SL can conceptually be distinguished into two components: an identification component (i.e., computing the TPs and extracting word forms from the speech stream, measured with neural entrainment) and a memorization component (i.e., transferring these word forms from short-term to long-term memory, measured in behavioral post-learning tasks; Batterink & Paller, 2017). An explanation for our mixed neural and behavioral results could be that the DD population has difficulties with this memory transfer process, but not with the identification component of SL. This would agree with work by Ballan et al. (2023), which has shown poorer consolidation of acquired statistical regularities into long-term memory for individuals with DD. Further work in that direction is necessary to conclude whether or not the memorization component of SL is affected in individuals with DD.

Another explanation for the brain-behavior dissociation in our findings could be psychometric in nature. Split-half reliability of the behavioral tasks assessing SL was not high (around .48 for both the rating task and TDT), comparable to an insufficient reliability of behavioral auditory SL tasks in the previous literature (e.g., Arnon, 2020, reported a split-half reliability of .43 in their first session with adults), whereas the reliability of the EEG data was good (.95 in an even/odd split, .78 averaged over random splits. This supports the view that neural entrainment during exposure is a more reliable measure of SL on the individual level than post-exposure behavioral tasks.

4.2. Group differences in mean scores on the tasks measuring individual differences

The results of our study indicated that the DD group obtained lower scores on the tasks measuring RA, WM, and vocabulary size, when group differences for all tasks were evaluated together. A visual inspection of these results (Figure 6) indicated that the standard deviations showed a large overlap for most tasks, while the means of the DD group on the Digit Span (measuring verbal WM) and the PPVT (measuring age-normed vocabulary size) were approximately one standard deviation below the mean of the TR group. This suggests that the effect may be primarily driven by the scores on the Digit Span and PPVT, rather than scores on tasks measuring RA or musicality.

4.2.1. No clear evidence for a rhythmic impairment in DD

Our results do not indicate clear rhythmic impairments in DD, contrasting with findings reported in the literature consisting of both behavioral (e.g., Bégel et al., 2022; Boll-Avetisyan et al., 2020; Caccia & Lorusso, 2021; Flaugnacco et al., 2014; Huss et al., 2011) and neural investigations (e.g., Chang et al., 2021; Colling et al., 2017; Peter et al., 2023; Power et al., 2013). However, this discrepancy might be dependent on other factors, such as differences in the tasks and age groups that were assessed in these previous studies. To our knowledge, only Bégel et al. (2022) employed a type of beat alignment task -similar to our CA-BAT -to investigate DD and TR group differences. However, their task was not identical to the one we used, and their investigation focused on children. We were unable to find publications comparing DD and TR groups on the rhythm and accent sub-tests of the PROMS.

In general, differences between tasks used to measure RA could contribute to differences between studies investigating RA. For instance, in our previous publication involving part of the TR group from the current study (van der Wulp et al., 2025), we found that the scores on the PROMS (Zentner & Strauss, 2017) and CA-BAT (Harrison & Müllensiefen, 2018b , 2018a) correlated positively only after we included more than 90 participants, showing inconclusive evidence with smaller samples. These tasks both aim to measure RA, but do so in quite different ways (i.e., comparing rhythmic sequences in the PROMS versus assessing beat alignment of a metronome to naturalistic music in the CA-BAT).

RA is also often measured as the accuracy of sensorimotor synchronization, most commonly through finger-tapping tasks (e.g., Bégel et al., 2022). We employed the SSS task (Assaneo et al., 2019) as a sensorimotor synchronization task, which correlated highly with the CA-BAT and the Gold-MSI but not with the PROMS in the typical population (van der Wulp et al., 2025). Taken together, differences in task demands contribute to differing findings regarding (impaired) RA in diverse groups.

Theoretical frameworks positing that individuals with DD have impaired RA argue that this is related to inefficient neural entrainment to auditory rhythmic stimuli (e.g., PRISM; Fiveash et al., 2021; Temporal Sampling Framework; Goswami, 2011; Atypical Rhythm Risk Hypothesis; Ladányi et al., 2020). These frameworks make predictions on the neural level, while we employed behavioral tasks as a proxy for RA. Neural processing of rhythms may not necessarily translate to behavioral tasks measuring RA such as the ones administered in the current study. Future work could further investigate how neural processing of auditory rhythms is related to behavioral tasks measuring RA in populations with and without DD.

4.2.2. Lower mean scores in the DD group on working memory span and vocabulary size

We found indications for group differences in WM capacity, with the DD group showing a smaller WM span as indicated by scores on the Digit Span being almost one standard deviation lower than in the TR group (Figure 6). This result is in line with our predictions and the previous literature reporting that individuals with DD have smaller phonological WM spans persisting into adulthood (Gabay et al., 2015; Smith-Spark & Fisk, 2007). Still, similar to Gray et al. (2019), our DD group showed large individual variability in their Digit Span scores, with overlap in the ranges of scores between the DD and TR groups. Based on these results, we cannot say that WM impairments are universal in the adult population diagnosed with DD.

Future studies may want to focus on investigating individual differences in WM components within an adult group diagnosed with DD, similar to previous work with children by Gray et al. (2019).

The DD participants' receptive vocabulary sizes were smaller than those of the TR participants, as indicated by their PPVT scores, which were around one standard deviation below the TR group's mean. This is in line with previous research showing that adults who were diagnosed with DD in childhood have smaller vocabularies than their typically reading peers (e.g., Ransby & Lee Swanson, 2003). However, again, there was large individual variability within the DD group and overlap between the scores of the DD and TR groups. An average smaller vocabulary in DD may be due to less print exposure, as this is positively related to vocabulary size (e.g., Misyak & Christiansen, 2012; Suk, 2017). Future studies may therefore want to incorporate a measure of print exposure (e.g., reading frequency) as a covariate when investigating adult vocabulary size in DD.

4.3. No group differences in relations between tasks measuring individual differences and neural measures of SL

We explored whether the groups differed in their regression coefficients (i.e., steepness of the linear relation between predictor and dependent variable) between the tasks measuring individual differences and the neural measure of SL (maximal ITCword in the structured condition). Our hypothesis was that a relation between RA or WM and SL, if found, would be the same for both groups, which predicts that the coefficients would not differ between the groups. In that case, difficulties with SL in the DD group could be (partially) explained by impairments in RA or WM. Indeed, we found statistical evidence for equality of the regression coefficients. However, this result became inconclusive in our sensitivity analysis. Hoijtink, Mulder, et al. (2019) argue that robust evidence is needed before any hypothesis is preferred over the null hypothesis specifying that there are no group differences. In our case, we cannot conclude that we found statistical evidence for differences regarding the regression coefficients between the groups, but we can also not conclude that there are no differences at all. Upon visual inspection of the coefficients per group (Figure 7), we established that the credible intervals showed overlap in most cases. This points to individual variability -rather than a group distinction -and likely is the reason we found inconclusive evidence for the hypothesis that the coefficients did not differ between the groups.

4.4. Exploring individual differences in SL in the combined sample

Our group comparisons suggest that the DD group on average reached similar maximal sensitivity to the TP-structure (i.e., the identification component of SL) to segment the speech stream in the structured language condition, and that the groups did not differ regarding the relations between individual difference measures and SL. Therefore, we exploratively investigated individual differences in SL in the combined sample including all participants from both groups together as one population (N = 143). The best model predicting individual differences in the maximal ITCword initially included very small positive contributions to SL from the Digit Span and SSS PLV, but the null model became the best model in the sensitivity analyses. Taken together, it seems that WM and sensorimotor synchronization have small positive effects on SL (as indicated by the maximal neural entrainment to the word frequency) in our combined sample.

Overall, our results suggest that the identification component of SL is largely independent from other cognitive abilities such as RA and WM in both typical readers and individuals with DD. This is in line with the account that SL ability is independent of general cognitive abilities such as general intelligence (Siegelman & Frost, 2015). We extended this line of research on possible cognitive factors interacting with SL to musical and rhythmic abilities. Furthermore, we assessed SL not only with behavioral tasks, but also with neural measurements able to assess the identification component of SL during learning. In contrast, our measurements of RA relied on behavioral tasks, which may be less 'pure' than, for instance, neural entrainment to rhythmic stimuli. We recommend that future studies employ more direct (neural) outcome measures for constructs hypothesized to interact with SL.

4.4.1. Limitations and directions for further research

Studies investigating neurodevelopmental disorders have frequently focused on group comparisons, classifying the group with a certain diagnosis as 'one kind of individual.' The current study emphasized that individual variability is a crucial factor for consideration when investigating cognitive processes in neurodiverse populations compared to their neurotypical peers. As discussed by Mirman (2014, Chapter 7), individual differences are highly valuable when investigating a cognitive process such as SL. They are not just random variance but constrain a theory of a cognitive system by describing how the system's behavior can vary. A good theoretical account for SL should explain individual variation in SL in the typical population as well as in atypical populations. It could then very well be that individuals with a certain diagnosis are often outperformed by their neurotypical peers, but our results do not indicate that this is consistently the case for SL in individuals diagnosed with DD.

Our neural entrainment results suggest that SL for speech segmentation is not impaired in the population diagnosed with DD, but the behavioral post-exposure evidence is less clear.

The current study was limited in its sample of participants with DD, by relying on self-reported diagnosis status, and diagnostic heterogeneity in moment of diagnosis or (current) symptom severity may have contributed to these results. Future studies investigating SL in DD are therefore advised to take inventory of the full diagnostic profile of individuals with DD, complemented with an individual differences approach. This way, future studies can shed light on which factors could contribute to individual differences in SL within the DD population.

This can be done by, for example, assessing print exposure, phonological awareness, and reading performance per participant. For instance, phonological awareness was previously found to relate to SL ability in DD (Zhang et al., 2021). Due to the length of the experimental session in the current study (approximately two hours), we did not include tasks measuring phonological awareness or additional reading or writing tasks.

Since RA and general language abilities have been found to correlate in several studies, it is possible that factors such as phonological awareness can be predicted by RA. In turn, phonological awareness may then predict individual differences in SL. This is in line with the 'noisy chain' hypothesis put forward by Schmalz et al. (2021), stating that each intermediary step between a proposed underlying mechanism and the end-state of an ability dilutes the correlation coefficient between the low-level deficit and the end-state outcome. Future studies may want to investigate mediations and moderations with such intermediary factors influencing relations between cognitive constructs such as RA or WM and SL in a variety of populations.

4.5. Conclusion

We obtained statistical evidence for SL for speech segmentation in both DD and TR groups, with similar word-form learning during exposure in the EEG data. In the behavioral tasks assessing SL outcomes after the learning phase, the DD group obtained lower scores than the TR group, but the Bayes Factors pertaining to these differences were anecdotal. The DD group also obtained lower scores on tasks measuring individual differences in RA, WM, and vocabulary size, compared to the TR group. Visual inspection of these results suggested that this difference was primarily driven by the tasks measuring WM and vocabulary, rather than RA. Comparison of regression coefficients between a neural measure of SL ability and the tasks measuring individual differences did not provide conclusive evidence for differences between the groups in how these tasks related to SL. Finally, we exploratively investigated individual differences in SL by combining both groups into one sample. This revealed anecdotal evidence that individual differences in SL are weakly correlated with WM and sensorimotor synchronization, which, however, was not robust in our sensitivity analyses. Our results emphasize the importance of an individual differences approach, moving beyond group comparisons alone.

The stimuli were presented to the participants in three blocks of 4.5 minutes each (13.5 minutes per condition; see section 2.3.1), where each block consisted of 900 syllables (300 words). FollowingZhang et al. (2021), we divided the data into six blocks for a more fine-grained time-course analysis.

Results of the time trend analyses indicated that the linear time trend in the structured condition for the TR group improved the model (BF10 (0, 0.2) > 1000). The quadratic and cubic time trends did not (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.18, and BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.02, respectively). In contrast, the linear time trend in the structured language condition did not improve the model for the DD group (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.02). The evidence that the quadratic time trend for the DD group improved the model was anecdotal (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 2.33), and not robust against increasing the prior (see Appendix A.1). The cubic time trend also did not improve the model for the DD group (BF10 (0, 0.2) = 0.01). We retained the quadratic time trend for the DD group in the structured condition because it was the time trend that received comparatively the most evidence, as well as descriptively the most fitting (see Figure4for a plot of ITCword entrainment over time in both groups and conditions).

F3, F1, Fz, F2, F4, FC3, FC1, FCz, FC2, FC4, C3, C1, Cz, C2, C4, CP3, CP1, CPz, CP2 & CP4

In our preregistration for the current project(van der Wulp et al., 2024), we proposed a multiple group mediation model, which was conditional on the results of our study investigating neurotypical adults(van der Wulp et al., 2025). The results of that study indicated no direct effect of the SSS task on SL in the general neurotypical population, and hence, the mediation analysis could not be performed. Therefore, instead of a mediation model, we built a multiple group regression model.
